explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The LORD says, "Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger; the staff in their hands is My wrath." (Isaiah 10:5) So Assyria is the rod, and the staff in their hands is His wrath. That's a whole lot of heat packed into one verse.
Mercy is a lovely word, but it's not the one here. The verse says the staff in their hands is "My wrath." (Isaiah 10:5) A woe, a rod and a staff of wrath. Nobody in that sentence is getting a hug.

Close to something you'd hold up and wave around, but no. The verse calls the staff in their hands "My wrath." (Isaiah 10:5) The LORD is speaking about His anger here, not handing down rules. Easy to mix up when the word "staff" has your mind drifting toward shepherds.

That's right. The LORD says He'll send Assyria against a godless nation "to take spoils and seize plunder." (Isaiah 10:6) Spoils and plunder are what an army carries off after winning. So the verse spells out exactly what Assyria is sent to do.

Not this time, baker. Isaiah 10:6 says God dispatches Assyria against a people destined for His rage "to take spoils and seize plunder." The verse says it plainly, so the statement is true. Sometimes the simple read is the right one.

explanations.answer: To destroy and cut off many nations
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says it's in his heart "to destroy and cut off many nations." (Isaiah 10:7) God sends him on one mission, but Assyria is carrying a bigger plan in his own heart. That's a man who got handed a job and decided to freelance.

explanations.answer: To make peace with every nation
explanations.explanation: A peace treaty tour would've been a nice change, but that's not what the verse says. It says Assyria's intention is different from what God sends him to do, and what's in his heart is "to destroy and cut off many nations." (Isaiah 10:7) Peace isn't anywhere in that sentence.

explanations.answer: To bring the people back to God
explanations.explanation: No, baker. The verse says what's in his heart is "to destroy and cut off many nations." (Isaiah 10:7) Bringing people back to God isn't what he has in mind. His plan is much more about taking than turning.

Good guess, but the text doesn't say that. Assyria asks, "Is not Samaria like Damascus?" in a string of questions pairing cities together (Isaiah 10:9). The way he lines them up, his point is that they're alike, and he's the one who took them. I think he's saying one more city on the pile is no big deal.

Right. He pairs cities up: "Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?" (Isaiah 10:9) The point is that they're alike, not that one is tougher. I think he's bragging that he's already taken the others, so why would these be different?

That's the one. Assyria says his hand seized "the idolatrous kingdoms whose images surpassed those of Jerusalem and Samaria." (Isaiah 10:10) Images are idols, and he says theirs surpassed the ones in those two cities. So his brag is that he took kingdoms with bigger idols than these.

It sounds like a natural thing to brag about, but the verse goes another way. It says those kingdoms had "images" that "surpassed those of Jerusalem and Samaria." (Isaiah 10:10) Nothing about armies comes up here. It's the idols he's comparing.

Walls would make sense in a siege story, but the verse doesn't mention them. Assyria says the idolatrous kingdoms had "images" that "surpassed those of Jerusalem and Samaria." (Isaiah 10:10) So the comparison is about idols, not walls.
Yes, baker. He asks, "…will I not also do to Jerusalem and her idols?" (Isaiah 10:11) He's already done it to Samaria and its idols. In his mind, Jerusalem is next on the list.

Damascus is in the verses just before, so it's easy to grab. But in Isaiah 10:9 it's just one of the cities he compares. The final question is about what he'll do "to Jerusalem and her idols." (Isaiah 10:11) That's where he's headed.

Hamath does show up in his list of cities in Isaiah 10:9. But the question at the end of the speech is, "…will I not also do to Jerusalem and her idols?" (Isaiah 10:11) So Jerusalem is the word that fits the blank.

You got it, baker. The Lord says, "I will punish the king of Assyria for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes." (Isaiah 10:12) Arrogant heart and proud eyes. That's a whole attitude you can see from across the room.

If he were humble, we'd be reading a very different story. The Lord says He'll punish the king "for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes." (Isaiah 10:12) Arrogant and proud are the words. Humble never makes the list.

Nothing about this king sounds scared. The Lord says He'll punish him "for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes." (Isaiah 10:12) Everything he says in this passage is bragging. Fear isn't in the text.

Not quite, friend. The king says, "By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom, for I am clever." (Isaiah 10:13) Notice whose hand and whose wisdom he names. It's his own, not the LORD's.

Right. He says, "By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom, for I am clever." (Isaiah 10:13) He credits his own hand and his own wisdom. The LORD doesn't get a mention in his boast.

That's it, baker. He says, "Like one gathering abandoned eggs, I gathered all the earth." (Isaiah 10:14) Right after that, he adds that no wing fluttered and no beak opened or chirped. He's picturing it as easy as picking up eggs nobody is guarding.

Feathers fit the bird theme, but that's not the picture. He says, "Like one gathering abandoned eggs, I gathered all the earth." (Isaiah 10:14) Eggs, and abandoned ones at that. Feathers didn't make it into his brag.

Twigs would be fair for a nest, but that's not what he says. The line is, "Like one gathering abandoned eggs, I gathered all the earth." (Isaiah 10:14) So it's eggs he's gathering. He's pretty pleased with himself about it.

Right. The questions that follow are, "Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it? Does a saw boast over him who saws with it?" (Isaiah 10:15) An axe doesn't lift itself over the person swinging it. The expected answer is no, and that's the whole point against Assyria's bragging.

Not this time, baker. The passage asks, "Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it?" (Isaiah 10:15) The questions that follow it, about a saw, a rod and a staff, all point the same way. Nobody expects an axe to say it's the boss, so the expected answer is no.
Yes, friend. The text says, "And the Light of Israel will become a fire, and its Holy One a flame." (Isaiah 10:17) Fire and flame, right in the same line. That's a big change for a light.

A shield sounds like a natural fit for a Light, but the verse says something else. It reads, "And the Light of Israel will become a fire, and its Holy One a flame." (Isaiah 10:17) So the word is fire. Not a shield in sight.

Shelter feels cozy, and this verse is not cozy. It says, "And the Light of Israel will become a fire, and its Holy One a flame." (Isaiah 10:17) Fire and flame are the words. This one is not for sitting under.
Not quite, baker. The text says, "In a single day it will burn and devour Assyria's thorns and thistles." (Isaiah 10:17) A single day, not years. That's a fast fire.
Right. Isaiah 10:17 says, "In a single day it will burn and devour Assyria's thorns and thistles." Years don't come into it. One day, and the thorns and thistles are gone.

explanations.answer: So few a child could count them
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The passage says, "The remaining trees of its forests will be so few that a child could count them." (Isaiah 10:19) Forests that were once full of splendor, and now a child can count what's left. Think about how short that count would be.

explanations.answer: Just enough to build one house
explanations.explanation: That's a clever guess, but it's not in the text. The verse says the remaining trees will be "so few that a child could count them." (Isaiah 10:19) Building a house isn't mentioned. Just a very short count.

explanations.answer: One left standing on each hill
explanations.explanation: Nice picture, but the verse doesn't say that. It says, "The remaining trees of its forests will be so few that a child could count them." (Isaiah 10:19) Hills aren't mentioned. It's about how few trees remain.
